placeContext.headerLine: A county seat in Fujian, Ming China

role.text: In view because this Story happens here.
The port's older name was Yuegang, the Moon Harbour. The court made it a county seat and named it Haicheng when it opened the trade in 1567.
Ships sailed from here under licence. In 1589, sixteen of the 88 licences were for Luzon.
Its customs put a flat charge on ships back from Luzon, because they carried coin and little else, and coin paid no duty.
Many of the Chinese who lived at Manila came from this county and the two named with it, Longxi and Zhangpu.
The marker shows the present-day town of Haicheng. No Source we have read places the customs house or the anchorage of 1602.

role.text: In view because the ships of this Story sailed here and came back with its coin.
The Spaniards settled here in 1571, with silver from America.

spatial.targetText: Haicheng (Yuegang), Fujian · settlement precision · named by historians; the Spanish writers name only the province
spatial.routeStatement: Ships licensed at Haicheng sailed to Manila in the spring and came home with silver coin. Because coin paid no duty, the Haicheng customs in 1589 put a flat charge of 150 taels (a tael was a Chinese unit of weight used to reckon silver) on each ship back from Luzon, and 120 the next year. The silver the port took in fees and duties rose from about 3,000 taels a year around 1570 to more than 27,000 about 1599. That rise covers all the port's trade, not Luzon's alone. No Source we have read gives a figure for 1602.

connection.scholarlyStanding: Atwell (1982, 1998) and von Glahn (1996) both read Haicheng's rising duties as a sign of foreign silver coming in. Atwell names Japanese silver beside Spanish-American. The duty figures are one series, from the Chinese historian Quan Hansheng. We found no historian who disputes the reading.

mechanismText.text: The Spaniards settled at Manila in 1571 with silver from America, and Manila became one of the places Haicheng's licensed ships went.
By 1589 the Haicheng customs officers said that the ships came home with coin and little else. An English merchant's note of about 1608 says the same.
Haicheng taxed goods, and coin was not goods. In 1589 the customs put a flat charge on every ship back from Luzon.
Haicheng's merchants asked for more Luzon licences. Luzon had sixteen of the 88, more than any other place.
The silver the port collected grew several times over between the 1570s and the 1590s.
Historians read that as foreign silver arriving. Some of it came from Japan, and the figures do not separate the two.
The men who carried it were largely from this county and the two named with it.
This is how the trade at Manila fed the port's duties. The Claims it rests on are listed beneath it. One historian's page carries the central step.

participants.text: Customs officers at Haicheng, who complained of the coin and set the flat charge
Merchants of Haicheng, who pressed for Luzon licences
Traders who sailed each year, and their agents who stayed at Manila
Governors of Fujian, who defended the licensed trade
Spaniards at Manila, who paid in coin
From about 1599, the palace commissioner over the sea duties

connection.evidenceIndependenceNote: The flat charge on Luzon ships rests on one historian, von Glahn, whose own source we have not seen. That the ships came home with coin has a second witness, an English merchant writing at Bantam about 1608. The duty figures are one series from Quan Hansheng, printed by Atwell and quoted by von Glahn.

reverseDisclosure.body: Goods and people going from Fujian to Manila are the Manila 1602 Story's Connection. This one carries only what came back and what the port did about it.

connection.reverseRelationshipNote: A separate Connection, not an inversion of this one. It is in the Manila 1602 fixture.

jurisdictionLine.text: In 1602 Haicheng was a county seat in Zhangzhou prefecture, in the province of Fujian, under the Ming. A commissioner sent by the emperor had charge of taxes in Fujian; historians name him as Gao Cai. How far the county reached has not been researched, so no boundary is drawn.

readingPaneEmpty.heading: One moment, and how we know it.
body: Select the Event on the map, or in the list beneath it, to open its Story.

This Moment is Haicheng in 1602: the port where the licences for the Manila trade were issued, and the one Connection this pilot explains for it, the trade at Manila and the port's ship duties. Manila is drawn at the wider view as the port the ships sailed to. The Story goes on to 1603, when very many of the Chinese of Manila were killed.

Manila lies too close to Haicheng to be drawn apart, so the two share one ring; choose it to see both. Ships licensed at Haicheng sailed to Manila and came home with silver coin. Researched legs are drawn: Fujian to Manila and back, and Manila to Haicheng (two Connections drawn as one line), Peru by sea to Acapulco and west to Manila, and Manila by sea to Acapulco and by road to Mexico City. Sea legs are approximate. A dotted tie to Potosí is one historian's reading. Select a moment to go to it, or choose Manila, 1602 from the index.

segments.text: The port the English merchant names. His word is 'Chauchu'. His editor of 1900 guessed one city and a later historian another.
What the port looked like in 1602. Our nearest witnesses are of 1589 and about 1608.
Where the coin went after the customs house.
The charge on Luzon ships after 1590.
When Gao Cai came to Fujian, and whether he ever lived at this port.
Gao Cai's own account. None is among the Sources we have read.
The names of the dead, and their villages. No list is among the Sources we have read.
What a merchant, a sailor or a wife of Haicheng wrote in 1602. The voices we have are officials, in historians' English, and one local book of 1617 that we have not read.
